items.stem: In which years did the Belgian administration introduce ethnic identity cards in Rwanda?
items.markingKey: 1933–1934. Following a census in 1933–1934, cards classified every Rwandan as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the introduction of identity cards was significant for later violence in Rwanda.
items.answer: Cards fixed fluid social categories as permanent hereditary ethnicities, and in 1994 roadblock militias used them to identify Tutsi for killing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cards fixed fluid social categories as permanent hereditary ethnicities, and in 1994 roadblock militias used them to identify Tutsi for killing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "Hutu and Tutsi were completely separate tribes with different languages and cultures before colonialism." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They shared the Kinyarwanda language, religion, culture and territory; distinctions were social and political, and were hardened by colonial rule.
items.markingKey: They shared the Kinyarwanda language, religion, culture and territory; distinctions were social and political, and were hardened by colonial rule. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that the Belgians invented the categories Hutu and Tutsi from nothing. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The terms pre-dated colonial rule, but Belgian policy racialised them, fixed them on identity cards and used them to allocate power and education.
items.markingKey: The terms pre-dated colonial rule, but Belgian policy racialised them, fixed them on identity cards and used them to allocate power and education. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Hutu Revolution of November 1959, explain how it illustrates the long-term legacy of colonial ethnic politics.
items.answer: An attack on a Hutu sub-chief, Dominique Mbonyumutwa, triggered violence against Tutsi; Parmehutu won elections in 1960–1961 and the monarchy was abolished. Power passed to a Hutu elite that defined the nation in ethnic terms, Tutsi exiles multiplied and anti-Tutsi violence recurred in 1963–1964 and 1973.
items.markingKey: Context (An attack on a Hutu sub-chief, Dominique Mbonyumutwa, triggered violence against Tutsi; Parmehutu won elections in 1960–1961 and the monarchy was abolished.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Power passed to a Hutu elite that defined the nation in ethnic terms, Tutsi exiles multiplied and anti-Tutsi violence recurred in 1963–1964 and 1973. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the long-term legacy of colonial ethnic politics.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Mahmood Mamdani, Ugandan political scientist, When Victims Become Killers: Colonialism, Nativism and the Genocide in Rwanda, 2001

The colonial state did not create Hutu and Tutsi, but it turned them into racial identities: Tutsi as alien Hamites, Hutu as indigenous Bantu. Once identity was racialised, the political question became one of natives against settlers.

How far can Source A be trusted as evidence for the colonial origins of ethnic division in Rwanda? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: A respected, widely cited scholarly interpretation that places the genocide in its colonial and regional context. Limitations: It is an interpretive argument with a particular theoretical lens (nativism); it focuses on political identity and less on the economic and immediate causes of 1990–1994.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Hamitic hypothesis"?
options: The racist colonial theory that Tutsi were a superior people descended from migrants from north-east Africa, used by Europeans to justify Tutsi rule
A document recording a person as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, introduced by the Belgian administration in 1933–1934 and retained until 1994
The rebel movement formed in 1987 mainly by Tutsi refugees in Uganda, which invaded Rwanda on 1 October 1990
An extremist Hutu newspaper founded in 1990 and edited by Hassan Ngeze, which published the “Hutu Ten Commandments”
items.answer: The racist colonial theory that Tutsi were a superior people descended from migrants from north-east Africa, used by Europeans to justify Tutsi rule
items.markingKey: A. "Hamitic hypothesis" is the racist colonial theory that Tutsi were a superior people descended from migrants from north-east Africa, used by Europeans to justify Tutsi rule.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased from Mahmood Mamdani, Ugandan political scientist, When Victims Become Killers: Colonialism, Nativism and the Genocide in Rwanda, 2001

The colonial state did not create Hutu and Tutsi, but it turned them into racial identities: Tutsi as alien Hamites, Hutu as indigenous Bantu. Once identity was racialised, the political question became one of natives against settlers.

Summarise the argument conveyed by Source B in relation to the colonial origins of ethnic division in Rwanda.
items.answer: Colonial rule transformed existing identities into racial ones, defining Tutsi as foreign, which made later conflict a struggle between “natives” and “settlers”.
items.markingKey: Colonial rule transformed existing identities into racial ones, defining Tutsi as foreign, which made later conflict a struggle between “natives” and “settlers”. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "structural adjustment"?
options: The racist colonial theory that Tutsi were a superior people descended from migrants from north-east Africa, used by Europeans to justify Tutsi rule
A list published in Kangura in December 1990 that told Hutu not to trust, marry or do business with Tutsi
Kinyarwanda for “cockroaches”, the dehumanising term used by extremists for the RPF and for Tutsi civilians
Economic reforms such as devaluation and spending cuts demanded by the IMF and World Bank in return for loans, introduced in Rwanda in 1990
items.answer: Economic reforms such as devaluation and spending cuts demanded by the IMF and World Bank in return for loans, introduced in Rwanda in 1990
items.markingKey: D. "structural adjustment" is economic reforms such as devaluation and spending cuts demanded by the IMF and World Bank in return for loans, introduced in Rwanda in 1990.

items.stem: "The civil war began because Hutu attacked the Tutsi in 1990." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The war began with the RPF invasion from Uganda on 1 October 1990; the regime then targeted Tutsi civilians as supposed collaborators.
items.markingKey: The war began with the RPF invasion from Uganda on 1 October 1990; the regime then targeted Tutsi civilians as supposed collaborators. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the introduction of multi-party politics in 1991 contributed to instability.
items.answer: New parties competed with the MRND, but party youth wings became militias, the CDR promoted extreme Hutu nationalism and the regime used ethnic fear to keep support.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: New parties competed with the MRND, but party youth wings became militias, the CDR promoted extreme Hutu nationalism and the regime used ethnic fear to keep support. The regime faced ruin: the price of coffee had collapsed, the south was suffering famine, and the World Bank demanded devaluation. The RPF attack of October 1990 gave the akazu an enemy against which to rally a frightened and impoverished population.

items.stem: Using the staged attack on Kigali on the night of 4–5 October 1990 as an example, explain how the regime used the war to target Tutsi.
items.answer: Gunfire in the capital was blamed on the RPF, and the government arrested about 8,000–10,000 people, mostly Tutsi and opponents. The fake attack provided a pretext to label Tutsi as an internal enemy and to crush opposition.

items.stem: Under the Arusha Accords, what share of the new national army’s troops was to come from the RPF?
items.answer: 40 per cent
items.markingKey: C. The government forces were to provide 60% and the RPF 40%, with officer posts shared 50–50.

items.stem: Distinguish between the terms of the Arusha Accords and the situation in Rwanda in early 1994.
items.answer: The Accords promised power-sharing, army integration and refugee return; in practice the transitional government was blocked, militias were being armed and Hutu Power was rising.

items.stem: Sana writes: "The Arusha Accords failed because the RPF refused to sign them." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Both parties signed; implementation stalled because of disputes over the CDR’s inclusion, splits in opposition parties and obstruction by Hutu extremists.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "RTLM was an official government radio station." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: RTLM was nominally private, funded by akazu members and allies, which allowed the government to deny responsibility while it competed with state Radio Rwanda.
items.markingKey: RTLM was nominally private, funded by akazu members and allies, which allowed the government to deny responsibility while it competed with state Radio Rwanda. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using French military support for Habyarimana from October 1990 (Opération Noroît) as an example, explain the international dimension of the civil war.
items.answer: French troops were sent to protect French nationals but also helped the Rwandan army halt the RPF, and France provided arms and training until 1993. Foreign support allowed the regime to survive militarily, encouraging it to resist concessions and strengthening its army and militias.
items.markingKey: Context (French troops were sent to protect French nationals but also helped the Rwandan army halt the RPF, and France provided arms and training until 1993.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Foreign support allowed the regime to survive militarily, encouraging it to resist concessions and strengthening its army and militias. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the international dimension of the civil war.

items.stem: Using the Hutu Revolution of November 1959 as an example, explain the long-term legacy of colonial ethnic politics.
items.answer: An attack on a Hutu sub-chief, Dominique Mbonyumutwa, triggered violence against Tutsi; Parmehutu won elections in 1960–1961 and the monarchy was abolished. Power passed to a Hutu elite that defined the nation in ethnic terms, Tutsi exiles multiplied and anti-Tutsi violence recurred in 1963–1964 and 1973.
items.markingKey: Context (An attack on a Hutu sub-chief, Dominique Mbonyumutwa, triggered violence against Tutsi; Parmehutu won elections in 1960–1961 and the monarchy was abolished.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe the split of opposition parties into “Power” factions in 1993–1994 and explain what it reveals about the collapse of the political centre.
items.answer: Factions of the MDR, PL and others formed Hutu Power wings after Ndadaye’s death, such as Froduald Karamira’s “Hutu Power” rally speech of October 1993. Moderate Hutu politicians were squeezed between the RPF and extremists, removing the base on which power-sharing depended.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from interviews with convicted perpetrators summarised by Scott Straus, US political scientist, The Order of Genocide: Race, Power, and War in Rwanda, 2006

Radio did not create the killers; but it told them that the authorities wanted the killing, that everyone else was doing it and that there would be no punishment.

What is the message of Source A about the role of the media in preparing the Rwandan genocide?
items.answer: Radio’s main effect was to signal official approval, conformity and impunity rather than to convert people into killers.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Economic crisis was the main reason for the outbreak of the Rwandan civil war in 1990."
items.answer: Economic crisis weakened the regime, but the war was caused mainly by the unresolved refugee question and the RPF’s decision to invade.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: coffee price collapse and famine; IMF structural adjustment weakened the state; land shortage in Africa’s most densely populated country. Arguments against: the refugee question and Uganda’s politics drove the RPF to invade; authoritarian MRND rule; long-term ethnic discrimination since 1959. Supported judgement: Economic crisis weakened the regime, but the war was caused mainly by the unresolved refugee question and the RPF’s decision to invade.

items.stem:
Source B: Paraphrased from the “Notes on the Social Aspect of the Racial Native Problem in Rwanda” (the Bahutu Manifesto), written by nine Hutu intellectuals for the Belgian Vice-Governor General, March 1957

The problem is basically that of the political monopoly of one race, the Tutsi. In present circumstances this political monopoly is turned into an economic and social monopoly. We ask that Hutu be promoted to public office.

How far can Source B be trusted as evidence for the colonial origins of ethnic division in Rwanda? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: A key contemporary document by Hutu leaders including Grégoire Kayibanda, revealing the grievances and racial language that shaped politics before independence. Limitations: It was a political manifesto addressed to the colonial power, so it presents Tutsi as a unified privileged “race” and omits the many poor Tutsi; it uses colonial racial categories.

items.stem: "The Arusha Accords made the genocide more likely rather than less." With reference to specific historical evidence, discuss the validity of this view.
items.answer: The Accords did not cause the genocide, but without enforcement they intensified extremists’ fears and incentives to act.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: terms threatened the akazu and excluded the CDR; extremists prepared to destroy the agreement; UNAMIR too weak to enforce it; planning for violence pre-dated the Accords (Bugesera 1992); responsibility lies with those who chose genocide; the Accords offered a realistic path to peace if supported internationally. items.stem: Who took command of the RPF after the death of Fred Rwigyema in 1990?
items.answer: Paul Kagame
items.markingKey: D. Kagame returned from military training in the USA to lead the RPF.

items.stem: Which of the following documents of 1957 attacked the “political monopoly of one race, the Tutsi”?
items.answer: The Bahutu Manifesto
items.markingKey: C. Nine Hutu intellectuals, including Kayibanda, published it in March 1957.

items.stem: "The Arusha Accords failed because the RPF refused to sign them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Both parties signed; implementation stalled because of disputes over the CDR’s inclusion, splits in opposition parties and obstruction by Hutu extremists.
items.markingKey: Both parties signed; implementation stalled because of disputes over the CDR’s inclusion, splits in opposition parties and obstruction by Hutu extremists. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between RTLM and Kangura.
items.answer: Kangura was a print newspaper (from 1990) aimed mainly at literate elites; RTLM was a radio station (from 1993) reaching the whole population and, during the genocide, naming targets and locations.
items.markingKey: Kangura was a print newspaper (from 1990) aimed mainly at literate elites; RTLM was a radio station (from 1993) reaching the whole population and, during the genocide, naming targets and locations. items.stem: Nia writes: "The civil war began because Hutu attacked the Tutsi in 1990." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The war began with the RPF invasion from Uganda on 1 October 1990; the regime then targeted Tutsi civilians as supposed collaborators.
items.markingKey: The war began with the RPF invasion from Uganda on 1 October 1990; the regime then targeted Tutsi civilians as supposed collaborators. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between pre-colonial Hutu and Tutsi identities and colonial racial categories.
items.answer: Before colonialism the categories were linked to status, cattle and lineage and allowed some mobility; colonial rule turned them into fixed racial identities recorded on cards.
items.markingKey: Before colonialism the categories were linked to status, cattle and lineage and allowed some mobility; colonial rule turned them into fixed racial identities recorded on cards. items.stem: Explain why the Arusha Accords were seen as a threat by the akazu.
items.answer: They gave the RPF and opposition parties a large share of ministries and military posts and excluded the CDR, threatening the power, wealth and patronage of Habyarimana’s inner circle.

items.stem: Briefly describe the staged attack on Kigali on the night of 4–5 October 1990 and explain what it reveals about how the regime used the war to target Tutsi.
items.answer: Gunfire in the capital was blamed on the RPF, and the government arrested about 8,000–10,000 people, mostly Tutsi and opponents. The fake attack provided a pretext to label Tutsi as an internal enemy and to crush opposition.
items.markingKey: Context (Gunfire in the capital was blamed on the RPF, and the government arrested about 8,000–10,000 people, mostly Tutsi and opponents.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Source B: Paraphrased from Mahmood Mamdani, Ugandan political scientist, When Victims Become Killers: Colonialism, Nativism and the Genocide in Rwanda, 2001

The colonial state did not create Hutu and Tutsi, but it turned them into racial identities: Tutsi as alien Hamites, Hutu as indigenous Bantu. Once identity was racialised, the political question became one of natives against settlers.

Identify the main points that Source B makes about the colonial origins of ethnic division in Rwanda, using details from the source.
items.answer: Colonial rule transformed existing identities into racial ones, defining Tutsi as foreign, which made later conflict a struggle between “natives” and “settlers”.

The Arusha Accords were a triumph of diplomacy on paper. But by giving the RPF so much, they convinced the extremists that they had nothing to lose by destroying the agreement and those who supported it.

An historian is researching the Arusha Accords and the failure of the peace process. Explain the value and limitations of Source C for this research, with reference to its origin, purpose and content.

items.answer: Political factors – the war and the elite’s fear of losing power – were decisive, but economic crisis intensified them.

items.stem: "The colonial period was the most important cause of the Rwandan genocide." Discuss.
items.answer: Colonial rule created the conditions, but the genocide required choices made by Rwandan leaders between 1990 and 1994.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: identity cards (1933–1934) fixed ethnicity; Hamitic hypothesis defined Tutsi as alien; colonial favouritism created Hutu resentment. Arguments against: three decades of independent Hutu rule (1962–1994) institutionalised discrimination; civil war from 1990 and economic crisis; deliberate planning by Hutu Power extremists in 1990–1994. Supported judgement: Colonial rule created the conditions, but the genocide required choices made by Rwandan leaders between 1990 and 1994.
